1.1.title: Board mandate
1.1.question: Is AI oversight an explicit, minuted board or committee responsibility?
levels: No board ownership; AI decisions sit with individuals or IT.
AI reaches the board only reactively — an incident or client question.
Named board or committee responsibility, recorded in terms of reference.
Regular metric-backed board reporting against thresholds, acted on and minuted.
Oversight externally assured and benchmarked against peers and standards.
1.1.leading: Oversight is externally assured and benchmarked; improvement is continuous and minuted.

1.2.title: Roles and decision rights
1.2.question: Is there a named accountable owner for AI decisions, with clear escalation?
levels: Nobody owns AI decisions; adoption is ungoverned.
Informal ownership by whoever introduced the tool.
Documented RACI for AI decisions with named owner and escalation route.
Ownership operates in practice; escalations logged and reviewed.
Decision rights independently reviewed and refined on evidence.
1.2.leading: Accountability is unambiguous at every level, tested in practice, and independently reviewed.

1.3.title: Policy architecture
1.3.question: Are approved AI use, acceptable-use and escalation policies in place and current?
levels: No AI policies exist.
Draft or borrowed policies, unapproved or unread.
Board-approved policy set covering use, escalation and exceptions; owner named.
Adherence monitored; policies refreshed on regulatory or operational change.
Policy effectiveness independently assessed; a model others copy.
1.3.leading: Policies are current, understood, measured for adherence, and improved on evidence.

1.4.title: AI inventory and register
1.4.question: Is there a complete, maintained register of AI in use — including procured and embedded systems?
levels: Nobody can list the AI in use.
Partial, stale list held informally.
Complete register with purpose, owner, data and risk tier per system.
Register currency tracked; changes trigger review.
Register independently assured; reused commercially in due diligence.
1.4.leading: The register is assured, always current, and a due-diligence asset in deals.

1.5.title: Third-party and procurement governance
1.5.question: Is due diligence performed on AI vendors and models before and during use?
levels: Tools adopted on marketing claims alone.
Occasional questions asked; answers unexamined.
Documented pre-adoption due diligence covering security, fairness and documentation.
Vendors reassessed on change; findings tracked to closure.
Contractual obligations with audit rights; exit plans for critical dependencies.
1.5.leading: Contractual obligations with audit rights; vendor performance tracked through life.

1.6.title: Regulatory horizon scanning
1.6.question: Is there a process to track UK and EU regulatory change and act on it?
levels: Regulatory change discovered when it bites.
Individuals follow the news; nothing systematic.
Defined scanning process with named owner, cadence and a change log.
Changes trigger impact assessment and documented action within set timescales.
Anticipates change pre-enactment; briefs stakeholders before deadlines land.
1.6.leading: Changes are anticipated before they land; clients and the board are briefed ahead of time.

1.7.title: Independent assurance
1.7.question: Is the AI governance system independently reviewed or audited?
levels: No independent eyes on AI governance.
Internal self-review only.
Periodic independent review scoped and scheduled; findings recorded.
Findings tracked to closure; assurance scope risk-driven.
Continuous assurance cycle; results shared with stakeholders.
1.7.leading: Regular independent assurance whose findings demonstrably change practice.

1.8.title: Documentation and records
1.8.question: Is there a defensible evidence trail behind AI decisions?
levels: Nothing written down.
Scattered records of some decisions.
Defined record-keeping standard; decisions, approvals and reviews filed per system.
Record currency and completeness monitored.
Evidence trail withstands external scrutiny unprepared; s172 considerations minuted throughout.
1.8.leading: Records withstand regulator-grade scrutiny without preparation.

2.1.title: Risk identification and classification
2.1.question: Are AI systems classified by risk tier, including procured tools?
levels: No view of which AI carries what risk.
Obvious high-risk uses informally recognised; no method.
Documented classification aligned to AI Act tiers, covering embedded and procured AI.
Classification refreshed on change and reported via telemetry.
Independently reviewed; horizon changes pre-assessed.
2.1.leading: Classification is independently reviewed and regulatory changes are pre-assessed before they land.

2.2.title: Risk appetite
2.2.question: Has the board defined what AI risk it will and won't accept?
levels: No stated appetite; case-by-case decisions.
Implicit red lines, nothing written.
Board-approved appetite statement with tolerances per use category.
Appetite operationalised as telemetry thresholds; breaches escalate.
Benchmarked against peers and standards; revisited on cadence.
2.2.leading: Appetite is benchmarked externally and revisited on a set cadence with evidence.

2.3.title: Impact assessments
2.3.question: Are data-protection and fundamental-rights impacts assessed before deployment?
levels: No impact assessment before deployment.
Sporadic DPIAs where privacy risk is obvious.
DPIA screening on every deployment; FRIA process ready where in scope.
Assessments updated on change; findings tracked to closure, board-visible.
Independently assured; templates reused in bids and diligence.
2.3.leading: Assessments are assured or published, and reused as evidence in bids and due diligence.

2.4.title: Deployer operational controls
2.4.question: Is AI used per provider instructions, with input-data checks, monitoring and log retention?
levels: Tools used however staff see fit.
Some usage rules in some teams; no input-data control.
Documented use per instructions; input data checked; logs retained six months minimum.
Controls monitored via telemetry; deviations corrected.
Controls audited; lessons feed vendors and procurement.
2.4.leading: Controls are audited and lessons feed back into procurement and vendor management.

2.5.title: Risk treatment
2.5.question: Are identified risks actively mitigated, transferred, or accepted with sign-off?
levels: Risks noticed are lived with.
Ad hoc fixes after problems occur.
Every identified risk carries a treatment decision with named sign-off and dates.
Treatment effectiveness measured; residual risk reported against appetite.
Independently reviewed; near-misses drive pre-emptive change.
2.5.leading: Treatment strategies are independently reviewed; near-misses drive pre-emptive change.

2.6.title: Incident readiness and suspension
2.6.question: Can you detect, suspend, and report a misbehaving system?
levels: No ability to detect or stop a misbehaving system.
Informal 'turn it off' knowledge held by one or two people.
Documented suspension procedure with provider notification; reporting windows understood.
Detection monitored; suspension rehearsed; incidents board-visible.
Integrated with cyber IR and tested end-to-end; reviews change practice.
2.6.leading: Response is integrated with cyber IR, tested end-to-end, and reviews change practice.

2.7.title: Ongoing monitoring
2.7.question: Is risk reassessed through the lifecycle, not just at adoption?
levels: Risk considered only at purchase, if at all.
Occasional re-checks after problems.
Scheduled lifecycle reviews with defined out-of-cycle triggers.
Continuous telemetry monitoring against thresholds; reviews minuted.
Benchmarked and assured; feeds horizon scanning.
2.7.leading: Monitoring outputs are benchmarked, assured, and feed horizon scanning.

2.8.title: Proportionality and documentation
2.8.question: Is the risk approach scaled to your size and context, and evidenced?
levels: Nothing written down.
Scattered records; effort mismatched to risk.
Proportionate documentation using simplified formats where the regime allows; a file per system.
Documentation currency tracked; gaps surfaced.
Withstands audit; reused commercially as a trust asset.
2.8.leading: Documentation withstands external audit and wins bids as a trust asset.

3.1.title: Discrimination risk awareness
3.1.question: Are protected characteristics mapped against your AI uses?
levels: No awareness that AI can discriminate.
Awareness in HR only.
Documented mapping of AI uses to protected characteristics; owner named.
Mapping refreshed on change; exposure reported to board.
Independently reviewed; informs design up front.
3.1.leading: Mapping is independently reviewed and shapes design before deployment, not after.

3.2.title: Bias in data
3.2.question: Is data screened for historical bias, including proxy variables, before it drives decisions?
levels: Data used as found.
Known-bad fields removed ad hoc.
Documented screening step including proxies before any decision use.
Screening results logged and monitored over time.
Methodology assured; lawful bias-detection carve-out used deliberately.
3.2.leading: Screening methodology is assured; bias-detection processing is used deliberately and lawfully.

3.3.title: Bias testing
3.3.question: Are outcomes tested for disparate impact across groups?
levels: No outcome testing; complaints are the only detector.
One-off checks without thresholds or records.
Defined disparate-impact testing at deployment; thresholds set; results recorded.
Recurring, telemetry-tracked; breaches escalate.
Independently audited; methods published to buyers.
3.3.leading: Testing is independently audited and methods are published to buyers as a trust asset.

3.4.title: Special-category data controls
3.4.question: Are restrictions on sensitive-data automated decisions enforced?
levels: Sensitive data flows into automated decisions unchecked.
Informal avoidance without rules.
Documented rule: no solely-automated significant decisions on sensitive data absent explicit consent or legal authorisation.
Controls technically enforced and monitored.
Assured; exceptions register reviewed by board.
3.4.leading: Controls are assured, exceptions carry justification, and the board reviews the register.

3.5.title: Meaningful human review
3.5.question: Do reviewers have competence, authority, and access to the system's reasoning?
levels: Rubber-stamping; reviewers approve what the system says.
Review exists but reviewers cannot access reasoning.
Reviewers documented as competent, authorised to override, with reasoning access.
Override rates and review quality monitored.
Effectiveness independently tested; feeds redesign.
3.5.leading: Review effectiveness is independently tested and feeds training and redesign.

3.6.title: Ethical review
3.6.question: Is there a gate where ethical concerns can stop a deployment?
levels: No ethical gate exists.
Concerns raised informally with no route to a decision.
Defined review step with power to require changes or refuse deployment.
Reviews minuted, tracked, board-visible.
External input or assurance; learnings published internally.
3.6.leading: External ethics input; learnings shared and demonstrably change decisions.

3.7.title: Vendor fairness assurance
3.7.question: Are supplier fairness claims verified rather than accepted?
levels: Vendor claims taken on trust.
Fairness asked about; answers unexamined.
Procurement requires documented fairness evidence before adoption.
Evidence periodically re-verified.
Contractual obligations with audit rights; performance tracked.
3.7.leading: Contractual fairness obligations with audit rights; vendor performance tracked.

3.8.title: Remediation and redress
3.8.question: When unfairness is found, is it fixed and are affected people made whole?
levels: No route to fix unfair outcomes.
Fixes made quietly; affected individuals not told.
Documented process: correct the system, review affected decisions, remediate individuals.
Timeliness measured; recurrence tracked.
Independently assessed; public commitment honoured.
3.8.leading: Redress is independently assessed and a publicly stated commitment honoured in practice.

4.1.title: AI-interaction disclosure
4.1.question: Do people know when they are interacting with a machine?
levels: Chatbots pose as humans by silence.
Disclosure only where someone thought of it.
Documented disclosure standard for all interactive AI; wording approved.
Coverage monitored across channels.
User-tested; exceeds the legal floor.
4.1.leading: Disclosure is user-tested and exceeds the legal floor across every channel.

4.2.title: Synthetic-content marking
4.2.question: Is generated content machine-readably marked and labelled where required?
levels: No marking of generated content.
Visible labels only; no machine-readable layer.
Layered marking (metadata plus watermarking) for in-scope systems; legacy deadline planned.
Robustness tested; compliance tracked.
Code-of-practice aligned; detection maintained.
4.2.leading: Marking aligns to the Transparency Code of Practice with detection capability maintained.

4.3.title: Decision-specific explanation
4.3.question: Can you explain this decision to this person, beyond boilerplate?
levels: 'The computer said no.'
Generic privacy-notice language only.
Capability to state main factors and logic per significant decision, in plain language.
Explanation quality sampled and measured.
Systematised explanation types, user-tested.
4.3.leading: Explanation types are systematised and tested with the people they are written for.

4.4.title: Contestability
4.4.question: Can people make representations, obtain human intervention, and contest decisions?
levels: No route to challenge automated outcomes.
Complaints channel exists, disconnected from the decision system.
All four safeguards operational: inform, representations, intervention, contest.
Volumes, outcomes and turnaround measured.
Independently assessed; learnings drive improvement.
4.4.leading: Routes are independently assessed and learnings feed system improvement.

4.5.title: Explainability by design
4.5.question: Is explainability a procurement and build requirement, not an afterthought?
levels: Black boxes bought blind.
Explainability a nice-to-have in selection.
Procurement requires documentation sufficient to meet explanation duties before adoption.
Vendor documentation currency tracked.
Contractual obligations; records kept beyond mandate.
4.5.leading: Contractual explainability obligations; transparency records kept beyond mandate.

4.6.title: Internal transparency
4.6.question: Does the organisation itself know what its AI does?
levels: Nobody can describe what the AI does.
Partial understanding held by individuals.
Complete register with purpose, logic summary, data and owner per system.
Register currency tracked via telemetry.
Assured; a due-diligence asset.
4.6.leading: The register is assured and functions as a due-diligence asset.

4.7.title: Notification of automated decisions
4.7.question: Are people told when significant automated decisions affect them?
levels: People affected unknowingly.
Notification buried in terms and conditions.
Documented practice of informing individuals subject to significant automated decisions.
Notification coverage measured.
Proactive and plain-language; trust measured.
4.7.leading: Proactive plain-language notification that measurably builds trust.

4.8.title: External reporting honesty
4.8.question: Do public claims about your AI match technical reality?
levels: Marketing writes cheques the technology cannot cash.
Claims published unreviewed.
Public AI claims verified against reality before publication; sign-off named.
Claims audited periodically; corrections issued.
Independently assured.
4.8.leading: External AI reporting is independently assured — the antidote to AI-washing exposure.

5.1.title: Automated-decision scoping
5.1.question: Do you know which decisions are significant and solely automated?
levels: No concept of automated-decision scope.
Obvious cases spotted informally.
Documented scoping: significance test plus meaningful-involvement test, applied to all systems.
Scoping refreshed on change; register-linked.
Tested against guidance as it finalises; regulations pre-tracked.
5.1.leading: Scoping is tested against final guidance and future regulations are pre-tracked.

5.2.title: Safeguards implementation
5.2.question: Are the four statutory safeguards genuinely operational?
levels: No safeguards exist.
Safeguards on paper with no mechanism.
All four rights operational with processes, wording and owners.
Usage and turnaround measured via telemetry.
Independently assessed; drive design.
5.2.leading: Safeguards are independently assessed as effective and shape product design.

5.3.title: Lawful basis
5.3.question: Is there a valid basis for training, inputs and outputs?
levels: Basis never considered for AI processing.
Blanket legitimate-interests claim, untested.
Documented basis per purpose with balancing tests; excluded bases never used for automated decisions.
Bases reviewed on change of purpose; drift caught.
Assured; withstands scrutiny.
5.3.leading: Basis analysis is assured and withstands regulator scrutiny.

5.4.title: DPIA discipline
5.4.question: Are DPIAs triggered, done well, and acted on?
levels: No impact assessments.
DPIAs as retrospective paperwork.
Screening on all AI; full DPIA for automated decisions and profiling; mitigations closed.
Currency and action-closure tracked.
Assured; reused as evidence.
5.4.leading: DPIAs are assured and reused as bid and due-diligence evidence.

5.5.title: Special-category handling
5.5.question: Are prohibitions and narrow exceptions for sensitive data correctly applied?
levels: Sensitive data in automated decisions unchecked.
Informal avoidance.
Documented compliance: default prohibition, narrow exceptions, technical enforcement where possible.
Monitored; exceptions logged with justification.
Independently assured; zero surprises.
5.5.leading: Independently assured with a zero-surprise posture.

5.6.title: Data quality and minimisation
5.6.question: Is AI fed relevant, representative, minimal data?
levels: Everything in; quality unknown.
Cleansing only where errors bite commercially.
Documented relevance, representativeness and minimisation standards for controlled data.
Quality metrics tracked; degradation alerts.
Assured; feeds fairness testing.
5.6.leading: The quality regime is assured and feeds fairness testing.

5.7.title: Rights readiness
5.7.question: Can access, erasure and objection requests be honoured where AI is involved?
levels: Rights requests break where AI is involved.
Manual heroics per request.
Documented processes covering AI contexts within statutory timescales.
Turnaround and completeness measured.
Assured; a stated commitment.
5.7.leading: Rights readiness is assured and a stated trust commitment.

5.8.title: Records and accountability
5.8.question: Does the data trail evidence all of the above?
levels: No records kept.
Scattered records.
A defensible accountability file per system: scoping, basis, DPIA, safeguards, decisions.
File currency tracked via telemetry.
Withstands regulator-grade scrutiny unprepared.
5.8.leading: Files withstand assessment-notice-grade scrutiny without scramble.

6.1.title: AI threat awareness
6.1.question: Are AI-specific attacks understood and mapped for your systems?
levels: AI treated as ordinary software.
Generic cyber awareness only.
Documented AI threat model: poisoning, adversarial inputs, injection, theft, leakage.
Refreshed against live intelligence; monitored.
Red-teamed; findings drive design.
6.1.leading: Systems are red-teamed and findings drive design.

6.2.title: Secure development and procurement
6.2.question: Is AI built and bought to secure-by-design standards?
levels: No security bar for AI.
Vendor questionnaires with unread answers.
Documented standards aligned to national secure-AI guidance for build and procurement.
Compliance verified, not assumed.
Independently assessed; contractual obligations.
6.2.leading: Independently assessed with contractual security obligations and audit rights.

6.3.title: Access and change control
6.3.question: Who can touch models, prompts and data pipelines — and is it logged?
levels: Anyone can change anything.
Basic access control without AI-specific scope.
Defined control over models, prompts, training data and pipelines; changes attributable.
Anomalies monitored; reviews scheduled.
Assured; crown-jewel treatment.
6.3.leading: Privileged AI access is treated and assured as crown-jewel access.

6.4.title: Containment and kill-switch
6.4.question: Can any AI system be stopped quickly by people with authority to do it?
levels: No off switch; nobody knows how to stop it.
One person could, informally.
Documented procedure: triggers, authorised roles, dual authorisation, rollback, business fallback.
Rehearsed; time-to-contain measured.
Tested end-to-end; agentic containment designed pre-deployment.
6.4.leading: Containment is tested under realistic conditions; agentic systems get explicit containment design before deployment.

6.5.title: Incident response integration
6.5.question: Does AI failure route into rehearsed incident response?
levels: AI incidents invisible to incident response.
Response would improvise.
AI failure modes in the IR plan; reporting duties mapped with windows understood.
Scenarios exercised; detection-to-response measured.
Integrated and tested; learning loop closes.
6.5.leading: Fully integrated and exercised, with a closed post-incident learning loop.

6.6.title: Resilience and recovery
6.6.question: Can the business operate when the AI cannot?
levels: AI down means business down, unplanned.
Workarounds exist in people's heads.
Documented continuity per material dependency: fallback, degraded mode, recovery.
Fallbacks tested; recovery objectives measured.
Assured; concentration risk managed.
6.6.leading: Resilience is assured and concentration risk actively managed.

6.7.title: Supply-chain security
6.7.question: Are model, API and vendor dependencies security-assessed?
levels: Dependencies unknown.
Known but unassessed.
Documented assessment before adoption; dependency map maintained.
Reassessed on change; vendor incidents tracked.
Contractual assurance; exit plans exist.
6.7.leading: Supply-chain assurance is contractual, with exit plans for critical dependencies.

6.8.title: Board-level security assurance
6.8.question: Can the board honestly make its material-controls declaration for AI?
levels: Board unaware AI is in declaration scope.
Aware, but without evidence.
AI formally within the material-controls framework; declaration evidence assembled.
Effectiveness telemetry-fed; declaration rests on data.
Independently assured; defensible under challenge.
6.8.leading: The declaration is independently assured and defensible under regulator-grade challenge.

7.1.title: AI literacy
7.1.question: Can staff and contractors use AI competently — and can you evidence it?
levels: No training; tools in use anyway.
Ad hoc sessions without records.
Documented programme proportionate to roles, covering staff and contractors; records kept.
Coverage and currency tracked; refreshed as tools change.
Effectiveness measured; a hiring and development criterion.
7.1.leading: Effectiveness is measured, not just attendance; literacy shapes hiring and development.

7.2.title: Oversight capability
7.2.question: Are human overseers trained, resourced and empowered — not just present?
levels: Oversight is nominal.
Overseers assigned without training or time.
Overseers documented as competent, trained, authorised and supported.
Quality measured via override rates and sampled reviews.
Independently assessed; roles carry weight.
7.2.leading: Capability is independently assessed and oversight roles carry career weight.

7.3.title: Oversight by design
7.3.question: Are systems configured so humans can intervene effectively?
levels: Systems present faits accomplis.
Intervention technically possible, practically ignored.
Deployment standard requires intervention points, reasoning visibility and time to act.
Intervention usage monitored; zero-intervention systems investigated.
User-tested; feeds procurement.
7.3.leading: Oversight design is user-tested and feeds procurement standards.

7.4.title: Workforce impact assessment
7.4.question: Is job-change impact assessed and minuted before adoption?
levels: Adopt first, discover impact later.
Impact discussed, nothing recorded.
Documented assessment before adoption; stakeholder consideration minuted.
Predicted versus actual impact tracked.
Assured; informs strategy.
7.4.leading: Methodology is assured and informs strategy, not just compliance.

7.5.title: Worker information and consultation
7.5.question: Are workers and representatives informed before workplace AI goes live?
levels: Workers find out when it arrives.
Announcement, not consultation.
Documented practice of informing workers and representatives before service.
Feedback tracked and demonstrably considered.
Co-design; trust measurably higher.
7.5.leading: Co-designed with the workforce, with measurably higher trust for it.

7.6.title: Augmentation-first strategy
7.6.question: Is the default job redesign over elimination, measured accordingly?
levels: AI framed internally as headcount reduction.
Mixed messages without metrics.
Stated augmentation-first policy; metrics shifted to throughput and quality.
Augmentation outcomes measured and reported.
Externally credible; a talent asset.
7.6.leading: An externally credible track record that attracts talent.

7.7.title: Acceptable use and shadow AI
7.7.question: Do people know what they may use, and is unsanctioned use surfaced?
levels: Shadow AI everywhere, invisibly.
Policy exists, unread.
Clear acceptable-use policy with a sanctioned request route; shadow use surfaced safely.
Detection tracked; policy iterated on findings.
Catalogue so good shadow use approaches zero.
7.7.leading: The sanctioned catalogue is good enough that shadow use approaches zero.

7.8.title: Skill sustainability
7.8.question: Does AI use build capability rather than hollow it out?
levels: Deskilling unnoticed.
Anecdotal concern without response.
Retained-capability decisions documented: what stays human, and how it stays sharp.
Capability retention monitored; wellbeing surveyed.
Assured; capability grows with AI use.
7.8.leading: A capability strategy under which the organisation gets more capable as AI use deepens.

8.1.title: Value-chain position
8.1.question: Do you know which customers' reporting duties reach you, and what they may ask?
levels: Requests arrive as surprises.
Big customers known; obligations unknown.
Documented map of client reporting duties and legitimate data requests.
Map refreshed as clients and thresholds change.
Anticipates requests; the easy supplier.
8.1.leading: Requests are anticipated before they arrive; you are positioned as the easy supplier.

8.2.title: Basic sustainability data
8.2.question: Can you produce the Basic Module data set on request?
levels: No sustainability data.
Fragments — energy bills somewhere.
Basic data assembled and refreshable: energy, emissions, waste, workforce, safety, pay, conduct.
Collection systematised; refresh cadence tracked.
Published proactively; a sales asset.
8.2.leading: The basic report is published proactively as a standing sales asset.

8.3.title: Comprehensive readiness
8.3.question: Can you meet comprehensive-module requests where finance or major clients require it?
levels: Comprehensive requests unanswerable.
Answered by heroics per request.
Capability where warranted: strategy, value-chain emissions, targets, climate risks, human rights.
Maintained continuously, not rebuilt per request.
Assured; opens doors on its own.
8.3.leading: Assured comprehensive data that opens finance and enterprise doors on its own.

8.4.title: The protected-undertaking line
8.4.question: Do you know what you may lawfully refuse — and do you?
levels: Every request answered, however excessive.
Grumbling compliance.
Documented refusal position: beyond-scope requests declined with legal basis stated.
Requests and refusals logged; patterns tracked.
Held confidently; burden contained.
8.4.leading: The line is held confidently, cited by basis, and the burden measurably contained.

8.5.title: AI environmental footprint
8.5.question: Is the energy and resource cost of your AI use known and managed?
levels: AI footprint never considered.
Vague awareness compute costs something.
Documented estimate of material AI energy use, from disclosures or compute proxies.
Tracked over time; efficiency weighs in vendor choices.
Disclosed; efficiency a selection criterion.
8.5.leading: Footprint disclosed; efficiency a stated selection criterion — a credible Twin Transition story.

8.6.title: Sustainability data quality
8.6.question: Is ESG data collected once, well, and reusably?
levels: Data reinvented per request.
Spreadsheet archaeology.
Single dataset with owners and refresh cycles, mapped to standard disclosures.
Quality and currency tracked via telemetry.
Assured; near-zero marginal cost.
8.6.leading: An assured single dataset with near-zero marginal cost per new request.

8.7.title: Sustainability governance
8.7.question: Is someone senior accountable, with board visibility?
levels: Nobody owns sustainability.
Owned by whoever was asked last.
Named senior accountability with defined board reporting.
Board reviews performance on cadence with metrics.
Integrated into strategy and pay.
8.7.leading: Integrated into strategy and remuneration; externally credible.

8.8.title: Commercial leverage
8.8.question: Is ESG readiness converted into won contracts and better finance terms?
levels: ESG treated as pure cost.
Used reactively when a bid demands it.
Readiness deployed deliberately: bid libraries, client summaries, finance conversations.
Win-loss and finance-term impact tracked.
Demonstrable advantage; the cited case study.
8.8.leading: A demonstrable revenue and capital-access advantage — the case study others cite.

links.reason: Policies carry authority only when a board or committee with an explicit AI remit has approved them; without that mandate, policy is one manager's preference.
links.source: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024

links.reason: A board cannot oversee what it has not been told is coming; tracking regulatory change is what keeps the board's AI agenda current.
links.source: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024

links.reason: Setting risk appetite is a board decision, so there has to be a board body that owns AI before appetite for AI risk can be defined.
links.source: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024; FRC Corporate Governance Code Guidance

links.reason: Accepting a risk needs sign-off from someone entitled to give it; the board mandate fixes where that authority sits.
links.source: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0

links.reason: Board oversight is only as good as what the organisation can tell the board about what its AI does.
links.source: Bank of England SS1/23; ICO AI audit toolkit: governance and accountability

links.reason: The board shows it exercised oversight through the records kept; without the data trail, the mandate cannot be evidenced.
links.source: ICO AI audit toolkit: governance and accountability

links.reason: The board's declaration on material controls has to cover AI, which it can only do if AI is already within a board body's remit.
links.source: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024; Cyber Governance Code of Practice

links.reason: Workforce impact can only be considered and minuted before adoption if there is a board forum where AI adoption decisions are taken.
links.source: Companies Act 2006, s.248; UK Corporate Governance Code 2024

links.reason: A named owner can only be assigned to systems the organisation knows it has; the register is the list owners are assigned against.
links.source: Bank of England SS1/23; NAO, Use of artificial intelligence in government

links.reason: Someone has to be answerable for classifying each system and for the tier it is given.
links.source: Bank of England SS1/23; Bank of England and FCA, AI in UK financial services 2024

links.reason: An impact assessment needs a named person who commissions it and acts on its findings.
links.source: EU AI Act, Article 26; ICO guidance on AI and data protection (accountability)

links.reason: Deployer duties such as human oversight and monitoring must be assigned to named, competent people.
links.source: EU AI Act, Article 26

links.reason: Monitoring through a system's life lapses unless a named owner stays responsible after go-live.
links.source: Bank of England SS1/23; EU AI Act, Article 26

links.reason: A person contesting a decision needs a human with authority to review and change it, which is the escalation route this criterion defines.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 22A

links.reason: Policies have to cover the AI actually in use; the register shows what that is, including tools bought in or embedded in other software.
links.source: DSIT AI Management Essentials; NIST AI RMF

links.reason: Policies stay current only if regulatory change is tracked and fed into them, including the staged application dates of the EU AI Act.
links.source: EU AI Act, Article 113

links.reason: Acceptable-use rules are the board's risk appetite written down for staff; without a stated appetite the policy has nothing to enforce.
links.source: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024; NIST AI RMF

links.reason: Suspending and reporting a misbehaving system relies on an escalation policy that says who decides and who is told.
links.source: NIST AI RMF; NIST Generative AI Profile

links.reason: Policy is what requires teams to record and disclose internally how they use AI.
links.source: DSIT AI Management Essentials

links.reason: People can only know what they may use if an approved acceptable-use policy exists and has reached them.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 24; R (Ayinde) v London Borough of Haringey [2025] EWHC

links.reason: A proportionate approach has to be evidenced, and the register is the base record that evidence is built on.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 30; Bank of England SS1/23

links.reason: Knowing what your AI does starts with knowing what AI you have.
links.source: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard; UK GDPR, Article 30

links.reason: The register is part of the records of processing; a data trail with systems missing from it is incomplete.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 30

links.reason: Using a system as its provider instructs depends on obtaining those instructions and the right information at procurement.
links.source: EU AI Act, Article 25; Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI

links.reason: Checking a supplier's fairness claims is one part of vendor due diligence and needs the contractual right to test and audit.
links.source: Guidelines for AI procurement; ICO AI audit toolkit: contracts and third parties

links.reason: Explainability has to be written into requirements and contracts at purchase; it cannot be added to a bought-in system afterwards.
links.source: Guidelines for AI procurement; ICO AI audit toolkit: contracts and third parties

links.reason: A data protection impact assessment of a bought-in tool depends on information that only the vendor can supply, which due diligence must secure.
links.source: ICO, AI tools in recruitment: audit outcomes; R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058

links.reason: Honouring access and erasure requests where a vendor holds the data depends on the contract obliging the vendor to assist.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 28; ICO AI audit toolkit: contracts and third parties

links.reason: Security assessment of models, APIs and suppliers is the security half of the same vendor due diligence.
links.source: PRA SS2/21; NCSC supply chain security guidance; Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI

links.reason: Independent review tests whether impact assessments were adequate; the Bridges judgment turned on one that was not.
links.source: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058; DSIT Introduction to AI assurance

links.reason: Bias audit is one of the recognised assurance techniques; independent review relies on bias testing having been done and recorded.
links.source: DSIT Introduction to AI assurance

links.reason: Public claims about AI are credible when independently checked; assurance is what lets external reporting match technical reality.
links.source: DSIT Trusted third-party AI assurance roadmap

links.reason: An auditor or regulator can only review what has been recorded; assurance draws on the data trail.
links.source: Data Protection Act 2018, s.146

links.reason: The board's declaration on the effectiveness of material controls is stronger, and safer to sign, when it rests on independent assurance.
links.source: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024; DSIT Trusted third-party AI assurance roadmap

links.reason: Screening data for historical bias depends on documentation of where the data came from and how it was collected.
links.source: Gebru et al., Datasheets for Datasets; Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard

links.reason: Showing that directors had regard to employees before adopting AI depends on the decision being minuted and the papers kept.
links.source: Companies Act 2006, ss.172, 248 and 414CZA

links.reason: Risk classification can only be complete if the register it works through is complete, including procured and embedded tools.
links.source: Bank of England SS1/23; NAO, Use of artificial intelligence in government; NIST AI RMF

links.reason: The evidence trail behind AI decisions and the data trail are two halves of the same record; a gap in one shows up in the other.
links.source: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard; Cobbe, Lee and Singh, Reviewable Automated Decision-Making

links.reason: Independent assurance reviews the documented evidence trail; without it there is nothing to audit.
links.source: Bank of England SS1/23; NIST AI RMF

links.reason: Named owners and escalation routes derive their authority from, and report to, the board body that holds the mandate.
links.source: Bank of England SS1/23; Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government

links.reason: Risk tiers mean something only against a stated appetite; the board's view of what it will not accept, including prohibited uses, sets where the tier boundaries sit.
links.source: EU AI Act, Article 5; Bank of England SS1/23; NIST AI RMF

links.reason: Classification is what triggers an impact assessment; a system that has not been tiered will not be recognised as needing one.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 35; ICO, When do we need to do a DPIA?

links.reason: A tier given at adoption goes stale as the system and its use change; reassessment through the lifecycle keeps the classification true.
links.source: Bank of England SS1/23; NIST AI RMF

links.reason: Proportionality means scaling effort to risk, which is only possible once systems are sorted by tier.
links.source: Bank of England SS1/23; NAO, Use of artificial intelligence in government

links.reason: Restrictions on decisions using sensitive data can only be enforced where classification has flagged which systems use that data.
links.source: EU AI Act, Article 5; UK GDPR, Article 35

links.reason: An ethical review gate needs a rule for which deployments must pass through it; the risk tier supplies that rule.
links.source: NIST AI RMF; ICO, When do we need to do a DPIA?

links.reason: Deciding to mitigate, transfer or accept a risk is a judgement against appetite; without a stated appetite, acceptance has no test.
links.source: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024; NIST AI RMF

links.reason: The board's declaration on material controls has to say which AI risks are material, which follows from the appetite it has set.
links.source: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024; FRC Corporate Governance Code Guidance

links.reason: A rights impact assessment has to say who could be affected and how; the mapping of protected characteristics against AI uses is that input.
links.source: Equality Act 2010, s.149; EU AI Act, Article 27; R (Bridges) [2020] EWCA Civ 1058

links.reason: The ethical review gate decides on evidence, and the impact assessment is the main evidence put before it.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 35; EU AI Act, Article 27; Ada Lovelace Institute, Algorithmic impact assessment

links.reason: The data protection impact assessment is the established discipline that wider rights assessments build on; where it is weak, the broader assessment will be too.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 35; EU AI Act, Article 27; ICO, What is a DPIA?

links.reason: A completed impact assessment is one of the core records an organisation is expected to produce on request.
links.source: ICO guidance on AI and data protection (accountability); R (Bridges) [2020] EWCA Civ 1058

links.reason: Telling workers and their representatives what a system will do to them draws on what the impact assessment found.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 35; EU AI Act, Article 26

links.reason: Operational controls such as input checks and monitoring are the mitigations in practice; a treatment plan with no working controls is only a document.
links.source: NIST AI RMF; Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry, Volume 1

links.reason: How much control a system needs should follow from a documented view of its risk; proportionality sets the depth of operational control.
links.source: Bank of England SS1/23; ICO guidance on AI and data protection (accountability)

links.reason: A deployer can only follow the provider's instructions and interpret outputs if the system came with that information, which is what explainability by design secures.
links.source: EU AI Act, Article 13

links.reason: Keeping the logs a system generates is a deployer control; those logs are a large part of the data trail.
links.source: EU AI Act, Article 12; UK GDPR, Article 5

links.reason: Monitoring and log retention can be trusted only if access to models, prompts and pipelines is controlled and changes are logged.
links.source: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI; Data Protection Act 2018, s.62; ETSI TS 104 223

links.reason: Operating a system safely assumes its model, API and vendor dependencies have been security-assessed.
links.source: EU AI Act, Article 25; Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI

links.reason: Controls are operated by people; staff who cannot use AI competently will not apply provider instructions or spot bad inputs.
links.source: R (Ayinde) v London Borough of Haringey [2025] EWHC 1383; Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI

links.reason: A decision to accept or mitigate a risk holds only while circumstances hold; monitoring is what shows when the treatment needs revisiting.
links.source: HM Treasury Orange Book; EU AI Act, Article 9

links.reason: A risk cannot be mitigated if nobody can see why the system behaves as it does; explainability is a precondition for effective treatment.
links.source: NIST AI RMF; ICO guidance on AI and data protection (accountability)

links.reason: The impact assessment identifies the measures to reduce risk, and where high risk remains it requires consultation with the regulator before going ahead.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 36; ICO, How do we do a DPIA?

links.reason: The board can declare its controls effective only if identified risks have in fact been treated and signed off.
links.source: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024; Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry, Volume 1

links.reason: A misbehaving system has to be detected before it can be suspended; ongoing monitoring is the detection.
links.source: EU AI Act, Article 26; NIST AI RMF

links.reason: Suspending an AI system and reporting on time works when AI failure is already routed into the organisation's rehearsed incident process.
links.source: EU AI Act, Article 73; UK GDPR, Article 33; NIS Regulations 2018, reg. 11

links.reason: Suspension is a human decision; it happens only if the people overseeing the system are trained and have the authority to stop it.
links.source: EU AI Act, Article 26; NIST Generative AI Profile

links.reason: Testing outcomes for disparate impact is one of the checks lifecycle monitoring has to repeat, because bias can emerge after go-live.
links.source: EU AI Act, Article 9; ICO, AI tools in recruitment: audit outcomes

links.reason: An impact assessment is meant to be kept under review; monitoring is what triggers its update when the processing or the risk changes.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 35; ICO, How do we do a DPIA?

links.reason: Monitoring for drift and accuracy depends on knowing the data going in is relevant and representative; poor data quality hides or mimics model failure.
links.source: ICO guidance on AI and data protection (accuracy); Bank of England SS1/23

links.reason: Evidencing a proportionate approach relies on documentation of what each system is for and how it behaves, which explainability requirements produce.
links.source: Mitchell et al., Model Cards for Model Reporting; Bank of England SS1/23

links.reason: An organisation cannot show its approach is scaled to its context unless it knows internally what its AI does.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 30; Raji et al., Closing the AI Accountability Gap

links.reason: The documentation that evidences a proportionate risk approach is itself part of the record the data trail must hold.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 30; ICO guidance on AI and data protection (accountability)

links.reason: Risk treatment acts on what impact assessments find; without assessments, treatment addresses only the risks someone happened to notice.
links.source: ICO guidance on AI and data protection (accountability)

links.reason: Which deployer controls apply depends on the tier; high-risk systems carry duties that lower tiers do not.
links.source: Bank of England SS1/23; NIST AI RMF

links.reason: Screening data for bias needs to know which characteristics are at stake in each use, including proxies for them; the mapping supplies that list.
links.source: Equality Act 2010, s.19; ICO guidance on AI and data protection (fairness, bias and discrimination)

links.reason: Testing outcomes for disparate impact has to be run across specific groups; the mapping of protected characteristics says which.
links.source: Equality Act 2010, s.19; R (Bridges) [2020] EWCA Civ 1058; CDEI Review into bias in algorithmic decision-making

links.reason: The organisation stays liable for discrimination by a tool it bought, so it has to know which characteristics to press the supplier on.
links.source: Equality Act 2010, s.109; DSIT Responsible AI in Recruitment

links.reason: Outcome testing finds bias after the event; it is interpretable only when the data feeding the system has been screened first, and each informs the other.
links.source: ICO guidance on AI and data protection, Annex A; FCA Research Note on bias in supervised machine learning

links.reason: Checking data for bias usually means handling sensitive characteristics, which is lawful only within the special-category controls.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 9; CDEI, Enabling responsible access to demographic data

links.reason: A supplier's fairness claim can only be verified by someone who understands what bias in data looks like and asks to see the supplier's evidence on it.
links.source: ICO, AI tools in recruitment: audit outcomes; DSIT Responsible AI in Recruitment

links.reason: Using sensitive data to detect and correct bias depends on the narrow legal exceptions being correctly applied and documented.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 9; Data Protection Act 2018, Schedule 1, Part 4; van Bekkum and Zuiderveen Borgesius (2023)

links.reason: Data that is unrepresentative or excessive is a main source of bias; data quality discipline is where screening starts.
links.source: EU AI Act, Article 10; ICO, AI tools in recruitment: audit outcomes

links.reason: Verifying a vendor's fairness claim means testing outcomes yourself or examining the vendor's test results, so in-house bias testing capability comes first.
links.source: NYC Local Law 144 guidance; Raghavan et al., Mitigating Bias in Algorithmic Hiring

links.reason: Where significant decisions use sensitive data, the law restricts solely automated decisions; meaningful human review is the control that keeps a decision outside that restriction.
links.source: UK GDPR, Articles 22A and 22C; Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, s.80

links.reason: Restrictions on sensitive-data automated decisions can be enforced only once the organisation has identified which of its decisions are automated and significant.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 22A; Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 Explanatory Notes

links.reason: A person contesting a decision is entitled to human intervention; that right is empty unless the human review is meaningful.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 22C; Green, The Flaws of Policies Requiring Human Oversight (2022)

links.reason: People can ask for human review only if they have been told an automated decision was made about them.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 22C; ICO, AI tools in recruitment: audit outcomes

links.reason: Whether a decision counts as solely automated turns on the quality of human involvement, so scoping and human review have to be worked out together, starting with knowing which decisions are in scope.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 22A; ICO draft guidance on automated decision-making

links.reason: Human intervention is one of the statutory safeguards; the safeguards are not implemented unless the review is real.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 22C; ICO AI audit toolkit: human review

links.reason: Review is meaningful only when reviewers are trained, have time and can overrule the system; research shows untrained reviewers defer to it.
links.source: ICO AI audit toolkit: human review; Alon-Barkat and Busuioc (2022)

links.reason: Reviewers can only intervene where the system and the process were designed to let them see, question and override outputs.
links.source: EU AI Act, Article 14; UK GDPR, Article 22C

links.reason: The ethical review gate needs a triggering process and written evidence; the data protection impact assessment already provides both and can require a deployment to pause.
links.source: UK GDPR, Articles 35 and 36; ICO, When do we need to do a DPIA?

links.reason: A supplier's fairness claims can be checked only if the contract secured enough information about how the system works.
links.source: Guidelines for AI procurement; EU AI Act, Article 13; ICO AI audit toolkit: contracts and third parties

links.reason: People can seek redress only if they know AI was involved in what happened to them.
links.source: OECD AI Principles, 1.3; UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI

links.reason: Putting an unfair decision right starts with being able to explain that decision; without an explanation neither side can see what went wrong.
links.source: EU AI Act, Article 86; UK GDPR, Article 22C

links.reason: Contesting a decision is the route by which unfair treatment reaches remediation; with no working route, harm stays undiscovered.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 22C; Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry, Volume 1

links.reason: Redress depends on affected people being notified that a significant automated decision was made.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 22C; ICO draft guidance on ADM safeguards

links.reason: The statutory safeguards (information, representations, human intervention, contest) are the machinery redress runs on.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 22C; Lyons et al., Conceptualising Contestability (2021)

links.reason: The body that can stop a deployment on ethical grounds is also the natural owner of decisions to withdraw a system and put harm right.
links.source: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence

links.reason: Telling people they are dealing with AI and marking AI-generated content are two duties under the same provision; an organisation without a disclosure standard has no basis for a marking one.
links.source: EU AI Act, Article 50

links.reason: People can only challenge an AI-influenced outcome if they were told AI was involved.
links.source: OECD AI Principles, 1.3; UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI

links.reason: A person cannot make meaningful representations against a decision they have not had explained to them.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 22C; ICO, Explaining decisions made with AI, Part 1

links.reason: An explanation of a specific decision can be given only if the system was bought or built to produce one.
links.source: ICO, Explaining decisions made with AI, Part 3; Bank of England and FCA, AI in UK financial services 2024

links.reason: The explanation is owed to people who have been notified; notification is the event that starts the explanation duty.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 22C; ICO draft guidance on ADM safeguards

links.reason: Giving information about a decision is one of the statutory safeguards; they are not implemented without a working explanation process.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 22C; EU AI Act, Article 86

links.reason: The person overseeing a system needs the same decision-level explanation to judge whether to accept or override an output.
links.source: DSIT Ethics, Transparency and Accountability Framework for Automated Decision-Making

links.reason: The right to contest begins with being told a significant automated decision has been made.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 22C; ICO draft guidance on ADM safeguards

links.reason: The ability to make representations, obtain human intervention and contest are three of the four statutory safeguards.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 22C; Kaminski and Urban, The Right to Contest AI (2021)

links.reason: Human oversight can be designed in only where the system exposes enough of its reasoning for a person to question it.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 25; NIST AI RMF

links.reason: The data trail records what the organisation knows about its AI; it cannot evidence what has never been established internally.
links.source: UK GDPR, Articles 5 and 30; ICO AI audit toolkit: governance and accountability

links.reason: An organisation does not know what its AI does while staff are using tools it has not sanctioned and cannot see.
links.source: DSIT AI Adoption Research; University of Melbourne and KPMG, Trust, attitudes and use of AI 2025

links.reason: Telling people about a decision is the first of the statutory safeguards and the one the others depend on.
links.source: UK GDPR, Article 22C; Data Protection Act 2018, s.50C

links.reason: Using governance credentials to win business is safe only if the public claims are accurate; misleading claims to business customers are unlawful.
links.source: Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations 2008, reg. 3

links.reason: Public claims about AI can match technical reality only if the organisation itself knows what its AI does.
links.source: UK Corporate Governance Code 2024

links.reason: Whether a decision is solely automated depends on what the human reviewer really does; scoping is wrong if it assumes oversight that is nominal.
links.source: ICO guidance on automated decision-making; Green (2022); Alon-Barkat and Busuioc (2022)

links.reason: Sensitive data needs a lawful basis and then a further condition on top; the second cannot be met where the first has not been established.
links.source: ICO guidance on AI and data protection (lawfulness); ICO Enforcement Notice, Serco Leisure (2024); Information Commissioner v Clearview AI [2025] UKUT 319 (AAC)

links.reason: Safeguards attach to significant automated decisions; they can only be put in place for decisions the organisation has identified as in scope.
links.source: ICO guidance on automated decision-making; Article 29 Working Party Guidelines on automated decision-making and profiling

links.reason: The completed impact assessment, and what was done about its findings, is a core part of the data trail.
links.source: ICO guidance on AI and data protection (accountability); R (Bridges) [2020] EWCA Civ 1058

links.reason: An impact assessment has to judge whether the data is necessary and proportionate, which rests on data quality and minimisation having been examined.
links.source: ICO, AI tools in recruitment: audit outcomes

links.reason: Secure development and procurement requirements are written against known threats; a team unaware of AI-specific attacks will not ask for the right protections.
links.source: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI; UK GDPR, Article 32

links.reason: Deciding who may touch models, prompts and pipelines follows from understanding how they can be attacked or misused.
links.source: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI; ICO guidance on AI and data protection (security)

links.reason: Recovery plans have to cover the ways AI fails or is attacked, which only threat awareness identifies.
links.source: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI; Bank of England, Financial Stability in Focus: AI (2025)

links.reason: Access and change controls are far easier to enforce on systems built or bought with them specified from the start.
links.source: NCSC Guidelines for secure AI system development; ETSI TS 104 223

links.reason: The ability to contain or switch off a system has to be designed in or contracted for; it cannot be relied on if it was never built.
links.source: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI; Implementation Guide

links.reason: Supply-chain security is the same secure-by-design discipline applied to models, APIs and vendors brought in from outside.
links.source: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI; PRA SS2/21; Gu et al., BadNets (2017)

links.reason: A kill-switch is only as dependable as the control over who can use it and who can change the system around it.
links.source: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI; NCSC, Managing the cyber risk of agentic AI

links.reason: Many AI incidents start at a supplier; response works only if dependencies are known and vendors are bound to notify and co-operate.
links.source: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI; Cyber Governance Code of Practice

links.reason: The board cannot declare its controls effective for AI without evidence that critical services can withstand and recover from AI failure.
links.source: FCA Handbook, SYSC 15A; Cyber security breaches survey 2025/2026

links.reason: Falling back to manual operation when AI fails depends on people still having the skills to do the work themselves.
links.source: CAA Paper 2004/10, Flight Crew Reliance on Automation

links.reason: Workers and their representatives can only be told what a system will mean for them once its impact on their jobs has been assessed.
links.source: EU AI Act, Article 26; UK GDPR, Article 35

links.reason: A strategy of augmenting people before replacing them needs the role-by-role evidence that an impact assessment produces.
links.source: Companies Act 2006, s.172; TULRCA 1992, s.188; DSIT assessment of AI and the UK labour market (2026)

links.reason: Skills are sustained when the strategy keeps people doing meaningful parts of the work; a replacement-first approach lets them lapse.
links.source: OECD AI Principles, 2.4; World Economic Forum, Future of Jobs Report 2025

links.reason: Which sustainability data an organisation must hold is set by what its customers, lenders and reporting partners will ask of it.
links.source: Niemann et al., Data Requests in Value Chains (2025); OECD, Fostering convergence in SME sustainability reporting

links.reason: How far readiness needs to go follows from the organisation's position in other firms' value chains and public contracts.
links.source: PPN 006; PRA SS5/25

links.reason: Knowing where the legal limit on value-chain requests sits matters only once the organisation knows who is asking and in what capacity.
links.source: Directive (EU) 2026/470; Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1563

links.reason: Wider readiness on strategy, targets and climate risk is built on top of the basic data set; without it the rest is assertion.
links.source: EFRAG VSME standard; Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1560

links.reason: The limit on what larger partners may request is defined by reference to the voluntary standard's data set, so having that data is how the protection is used.
links.source: Commission Recommendation (EU) 2025/1710; Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1560

links.reason: Knowing what cannot be demanded lets the organisation aim its readiness at what is warranted, not at every request it receives.
links.source: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1560; PPN 006

links.reason: AI use adds to energy use and purchased-services emissions, so a full picture of readiness has to include the AI footprint.
links.source: Greenhouse Gas Protocol Corporate Value Chain (Scope 3) Standard

links.reason: Readiness claims rest on the numbers behind them; weak data quality undermines every disclosure built on it.
links.source: EFRAG VSME standard; Klaaßen and Stoll, Harmonizing corporate carbon footprints (2021)

links.reason: Readiness is sustained when someone senior is accountable and the board sees progress; disclosure frameworks ask for that governance first.
links.source: UK SRS S2; Companies Act 2006, s.414CB; FRC Thematic Review of climate-related disclosures (2025)

links.reason: Sustainability credentials win contracts when the organisation knows what buyers can legitimately require and offers that confidently.
links.source: PPN 006; Procurement Act 2023, s.12

links.reason: A figure for AI's environmental footprint is credible only if it is measured to the same standard as the rest of the organisation's energy and carbon data.
links.source: Greenhouse Gas Protocol Scope 3 Standard; Environmental Reporting Guidelines (SECR)
